requirement_text.REQ-160: Second of two sibling requirements splitting the platform.* surface; REQ-159 covers the read path. This one covers the functions with OUTBOUND EFFECT: their correctness condition is transactional, not per-call. LUA-11 write half (MUST): 'platform.write_variable(name, value) MUST stage a write; writes are applied atomically on script success and DISCARDED ON SCRIPT FAILURE.' Acceptance: 'Failed script does not leave partial variable writes in instance state.' A write_variable that applies immediately satisfies the function signature and violates the requirement. Staging must survive every failure arm S5 has built: sandbox violation, REQ-154's instruction budget, REQ-155's wall-clock kill, REQ-156's memory limit, and REQ-161's platform.fail. The kill arm is the sharp one -- a brutal kill of the execution process must not leave a half-applied write, which means the staging buffer cannot live only inside the killed process's own state UNLESS the apply step happens strictly after the process exits normally. LUA-12 (Service Call, MUST): 'platform.call_service(service_id, payload) MUST invoke a registered service synchronously. Response MUST be returned as Lua table. Service call failures MUST RETURN A STRUCTURED ERROR, NOT RAISE.' Acceptance: 'Calling a registered service round-trips through host.' Note the asymmetry with LUA-06: a MISSING CAPABILITY raises (LUA-06), a SERVICE FAILURE returns a structured error (LUA-12). Both behaviours must be tested and must differ. CAPABILITY GATES: write_variable requires variable:write; call_service requires service:call:<svc_id> (parameterised per service, per REQ-157); emit_event requires event:emit. NUMBER MARSHALLING: same constraint as REQ-159 -- use REQ-150's central conversion, cite its normative section, introduce no second rule. TENANT BOUNDARY: same as REQ-159 -- the tenant prefix comes from the calling engine code, never from script input. NOT IN THIS REQUIREMENT: platform.fail (REQ-161). GATE: SECURITY-REVIEWER is a hard gate. Queue task 312, GH#612. See docs/requirements.yaml REQ-160 for full description and acceptance_criteria.

task.description: CODE-DESIGNER (WF-02 Step 1) for REQ-160. Write lib/letflow/design/req160-lua-host-api-write.md. This is the architecturally hardest Lua requirement this session -- read lib/letflow/engine/lua/platform.ex in full (REQ-159's now-merged state, including the execution_context/install/3 mechanism and the 3 real stub replacements) and lib/letflow/design/req155-lua-wallclock-kill.md + req156-lua-memory-limit-impl.md in full (the two kill mechanisms this design must survive) before starting. THE CENTRAL ARCHITECTURAL QUESTION: where does a staged write live such that it is (a) applied atomically on script success, (b) discarded on every failure arm including a brutal external kill of the executing process? Investigate and verify (don't just assert) this hypothesis: since REQ-155/156's kill mechanisms terminate the SCRIPT-EXECUTING PROCESS itself (via Process.exit(:kill) or the BEAM's own max_heap_size enforcement) and the caller only learns the outcome via the process's normal return value OR a :DOWN monitor message, a staging buffer that lives ENTIRELY inside the script-executing process's own memory (e.g., accumulated via Process.put/get, or a value threaded through the Lua VM's own state and returned as part of the final result) is automatically discarded by any kill -- because the process's memory, including that buffer, ceases to exist along with it. On SUCCESS, the buffer only needs to reach the caller via the SAME normal-return path Executor already uses (the process's return value), which then gets merged into instance state via a single Letflow.Engine.VariableMerge.merge/3 call (read lib/letflow/engine/variable_merge.ex to confirm its exact signature and atomicity properties -- does a single merge/3 call already guarantee no partial-application-observable state, or does something else need to guarantee that?). This means 'survives a kill' may not require anything special at all -- it requires the OPPOSITE: making sure nothing escapes the process except through its normal, single, atomic return value. Verify this reasoning is sound by reading the actual REQ-155/156 kill code paths, and design accordingly -- or, if you find a flaw in this reasoning, design the correct alternative and explain why the above doesn't work. SEPARATELY, for call_service: search this codebase for any existing 'registered service' or service-invocation abstraction (grep for ServiceRegistry, register_service, service dispatch outside of ServiceTask's HTTP-service-task BPMN concept, which is a different thing -- a BPMN node config, not a Lua-callable service registry). If none exists (likely, confirmed no hits during ORCH's own pre-dispatch search), this design must specify a minimal INJECTED behaviour, mirroring LuaScriptAudit's Executor-behaviour pattern (an injected module implementing a callback, not a real dispatch mechanism built here) -- state this as an explicit, honest scope decision, not silently assume infrastructure that doesn't exist. Also specify: emit_event's real behavior (what does 'emit an event observable by the host' mean concretely in this codebase -- is there an existing event-emission mechanism to hook into, e.g. Letflow.EventStore? search and cite it, or flag as an open question). Design must also specify: write_variable's staging data structure and how multiple writes in one script accumulate before the single atomic merge; call_service's structured-error-vs-raise distinction (LUA-12 vs LUA-06) implemented as genuinely different code paths; the number-marshalling citation (REQ-150, from_lua/1 for the write direction this time, not to_lua/1); the tenant-prefix-never-from-script discipline (same as REQ-159). Also write test/specs/REQ-160.md (test spec skeleton, no test code). No implementation code (.ex function bodies) -- signatures, @specs, and type shapes only, describing control flow in prose/tables, never as a literal Elixir expression, however small (this rule has cost rework on most Lua-hardening designs this session -- grep your own draft before submitting).
acceptance_criteria: Design specifies where staged writes live and rigorously justifies (not merely asserts) that this location makes writes automatically discarded on every failure arm including a brutal process kill, and applied atomically on success via a single VariableMerge.merge/3-style call -- verified against the actual REQ-155/156 kill mechanisms' real code, not assumed
Design specifies call_service's structured-error-vs-missing-capability-raise distinction as genuinely different code paths (LUA-12 returns, LUA-06 raises)

Design honestly assesses whether a 'registered service' abstraction exists in this codebase; if not, specifies a minimal injected-behaviour design (mirroring LuaScriptAudit's Executor pattern) rather than assuming infrastructure that doesn't exist
Design honestly assesses whether an event-emission mechanism exists for emit_event to hook into; cites it if found, flags as an open question if not
Design cites REQ-150's number-marshalling rule by section number for the write direction (from_lua/1), introduces no second rule
Design states the tenant-prefix-never-from-script discipline consistently with REQ-159's precedent
Design covers all 8 acceptance criteria listed in docs/requirements.yaml's REQ-160 entry (read it directly), mapped one-to-one to concrete design elements

No implementation code (.ex function bodies) -- signatures, @specs, and type shapes only; describe control flow in prose/tables, never as a literal Elixir expression, however small -- grep your own draft for fn /raise /case /cond /do:/-> before submitting
Open questions listed explicitly if any exist, not silently resolved

REWORK ITERATION 1: CODE-DESIGN-VALIDATOR (step-01b, commit 0f3f809) returned FAIL. Everything else stands (all 8 ACs mapped, no literal code, VariableMerge.merge/3's atomicity independently verified, the LUA-06/LUA-12 raise/return split confirmed structurally real, the injected ServiceCaller behaviour confirmed honestly scoped, Letflow.EventStore.append/2's citation confirmed accurate, the deferred executor.ex wiring gap confirmed flagged as OQ-1) -- the ONLY defect is section 2.2's channel enumeration, which claims the caller's only channels into the killed process's outcome are (a) the normal return/message or (b) a payload-less :DOWN message. This is inaccurate: Task.shutdown(task, :brutal_kill) has documented Elixir behavior to return {:ok, reply} instead of :ok when the task's process already sent its normal-completion message before the kill signal landed -- a real third channel. The equivalent race exists on REQ-156's raw spawn_opt/monitor path (a late {ref, reply} message could sit in the caller's mailbox alongside or instead of the :DOWN message). REQ-155/156's current code happens to stay safe only because their timeout/memory-limit branches return the structured error unconditionally without ever reading what Task.shutdown/2 or the drained mailbox actually returned -- but nothing states this as a required, load-bearing invariant, and REQ-160's own deferred wiring (OQ-1/section 2.5) tasks a FUTURE implementer with extending the success-return shape to carry staged_variables -- exactly the kind of change that could plausibly pattern-match on Task.shutdown/2's legitimate {:ok, reply} idiom and let a killed script's staged writes leak through. FIX: (1) correct section 2.2's channel enumeration to acknowledge Task.shutdown/2's {:ok, reply} return and the raw-kill path's possible late {ref, reply} mailbox message as a real third channel, not assume it away; (2) state explicitly, as a hard invariant binding any future OQ-1/section-2.5 wiring, that on REQ-155's timeout arm and REQ-156's memory-limit-timeout arm, the structured error tuple MUST be returned unconditionally regardless of what Task.shutdown/2 or the drained mailbox actually contains -- a late-arriving successful reply on either of those two branches must never be substituted for the error tuple, even after a future wiring adds a staged_variables field to the success shape; (3) since this invariant is actually cross-cutting (REQ-155/156's own already-merged code is what must honor it, not code this run owns), state within REQ-160's own design that this is a cross-cutting invariant REQ-160's correctness depends on, name it precisely (e.g. INV-write staged-writes discard-on-race, or similar), and cite REQ-155 section 4.3 / REQ-156 section 5.2 by number as the exact branches that must honor it -- do NOT attempt to edit req155-lua-wallclock-kill.md or req156-lua-memory-limit-impl.md themselves (out of this run's owned_modules; a documentation-only addendum to those merged docs, if warranted, is a follow-up for a future run/DOC-UPDATER, not this design). Re-grep the whole document for literal Elixir code after editing. On finishing, flip this handoff's status to COMPLETED/FAILED as normal with a real result.
Open questions listed explicitly if any exist, not silently resolved
